questions.title: Build an Adjacency List
questions.objective: Represent an undirected graph with adjacency lists and sorted neighbors.
questions.problem_statement:
Given an undirected graph, build its adjacency list. List each vertex's neighbors in ascending order.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-01 — Build an Adjacency List](/diagrams/m19/m19_01.png)

Explanation: Vertex 1 is connected to 2 and 3, sorted as 2 3. Vertices 2 and 3 connect back to 1, while 4 and 5 form a separate component.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines each contain an edge u v.
questions.output_format: Print one line for each vertex i from 1 to N in the format i: followed by its sorted neighbors, each preceded by one space. If a vertex has no neighbors, print i: alone.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
The graph is undirected, with no self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: Each undirected edge u v must be added to both u's list and v's list.
Sort every neighbor list once after all edges have been read.
Build the whole output in a StringBuilder; printing 100,000 lines one at a time is slow.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines each contain an edge u v.
extra_fields.output_format: Print one line for each vertex i from 1 to N in the format i: followed by its sorted neighbors, each preceded by one space. If a vertex has no neighbors, print i: alone.

questions.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS) Traversal
questions.objective: Traverse a graph level by level with a queue.
questions.problem_statement:
Perform BFS on an undirected graph starting from source S. When exploring a vertex, visit its unvisited neighbors in ascending order.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-02 — Breadth-First Search (BFS) Traversal](/diagrams/m19/m19_02.png)

Explanation: BFS visits 1 first, then its neighbors 2 and 3 in ascending order, and then visits 4 from vertex 2. Vertices 5 and 6 are unreachable from 1.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v. The final line contains S.
questions.output_format: Print the BFS visitation order from S, separated by single spaces. Vertices unreachable from S are not printed.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
1 ≤ S ≤ N
No self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: Mark a vertex as visited when it is added to the queue, not when it is removed, so it is never queued twice.
Sort each neighbor list so neighbors are discovered in ascending order.
Only the component containing S is printed.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v. The final line contains S.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the BFS visitation order from S, separated by single spaces. Vertices unreachable from S are not printed.

questions.title: Depth-First Search (DFS) Traversal
questions.objective: Simulate recursive DFS with an explicit stack that remembers each vertex's progress.
questions.problem_statement:
Perform depth-first search starting from source S. Define the traversal as the order in which recursive DFS first visits vertices, exploring neighbors in ascending order.

Because N may be 100,000, do not use recursive calls. Use an explicit stack that stores each active vertex and its current position in its sorted neighbor list, so the result exactly matches recursive DFS. A plain stack that pushes all neighbors at once is not sufficient because it can produce a different order.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-03 — Depth-First Search (DFS) Traversal](/diagrams/m19/m19_03.png)

Explanation: From 1, DFS first visits 2. It explores 4, returns to 2, explores 5, and then returns to 1 to visit 3.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain undirected edges u v. The final line contains S.
questions.output_format: Print the DFS visitation order from S, separated by single spaces. Unreachable vertices are omitted.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
1 ≤ S ≤ N
No self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: Keep an array next[v] holding the index of the next neighbor of v to examine.
Look at the vertex on top of the stack: if it has an unexamined neighbor that is unvisited, visit it and push it; if it has no neighbors left, pop it.
Sample 2 shows why pushing all neighbors at once fails: from 1, recursive DFS reaches 4 through 2 before it returns to visit 3.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain undirected edges u v. The final line contains S.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the DFS visitation order from S, separated by single spaces. Unreachable vertices are omitted.

questions.title: Check Whether an Undirected Graph Is Connected
questions.objective: Decide reachability of all vertices with an iterative traversal or DSU.
questions.problem_statement:
Determine whether every vertex in an undirected graph is reachable from vertex 1. Use an iterative traversal or DSU; do not rely on recursive DFS for this input limit.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-04 — Check Whether an Undirected Graph Is Connected](/diagrams/m19/m19_04.png)

Explanation: Vertices 1 and 2 form one component, while 3 and 4 form another. Not every vertex is reachable from 1.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
questions.output_format: Print YES if every vertex is reachable from vertex 1; otherwise, print NO.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
No self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: Run BFS from vertex 1 and count how many vertices it reaches.
The graph is connected exactly when that count equals N.
A single vertex with no edges is connected.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
extra_fields.output_format: Print YES if every vertex is reachable from vertex 1; otherwise, print NO.

questions.title: Count Connected Components
questions.objective: Count components with repeated iterative traversal or union-find.
questions.problem_statement:
Count the connected components in an undirected graph. An isolated vertex is a component by itself. Use an iterative traversal or DSU rather than recursive DFS.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-05 — Count Connected Components](/diagrams/m19/m19_05.png)

Explanation: The components are {1,2,3}, {4}, and {5,6}, so the answer is 3.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
questions.output_format: Print the number of connected components.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
No self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: Start a new traversal from every vertex that has not been visited yet; each start is a new component.
With DSU, start with N components and subtract one for every union that joins two different sets.
Vertices with no edges still count.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the number of connected components.

questions.title: Detect a Cycle in an Undirected Graph
questions.objective: Detect undirected cycles with union-find or a parent-aware traversal.
questions.problem_statement:
Determine whether an undirected graph contains a cycle. A cycle is a closed path with at least three distinct vertices before returning to its start. The graph has no self-loops or parallel edges. Use an iterative traversal or DSU rather than recursive DFS.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-06 — Detect a Cycle in an Undirected Graph](/diagrams/m19/m19_06.png)

Explanation: Vertices 1, 2, and 3 form a cycle: 1–2–3–1.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
questions.output_format: Print CYCLE if any cycle exists; otherwise, print ACYCLIC.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
No self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: With DSU, an edge whose endpoints are already in the same set closes a cycle.
With BFS, reaching an already-visited vertex that is not the current vertex's parent means a cycle.
Check every component, not only the one containing vertex 1.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
extra_fields.output_format: Print CYCLE if any cycle exists; otherwise, print ACYCLIC.

questions.title: Detect a Cycle in a Directed Graph
questions.objective: Detect directed cycles with Kahn's algorithm or three-color DFS.
questions.problem_statement:
Determine whether a directed graph contains a directed cycle. A directed cycle follows every edge in its arrow direction.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-07 — Detect a Cycle in a Directed Graph](/diagrams/m19/m19_07.png)

Explanation: The directed edges 1 -> 2, 2 -> 3, and 3 -> 1 return to vertex 1, forming a directed cycle.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain directed edges u v, meaning u -> v.
questions.output_format: Print CYCLE if a directed cycle exists; otherwise, print ACYCLIC.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 5,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 20,000
No self-loops or duplicate directed edges.
hints: An undirected cycle is not necessarily a directed cycle: 1 -> 2, 2 -> 3, 1 -> 3 is acyclic.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove vertices with indegree 0. If some vertices are never removed, a cycle exists.
With DFS, a cycle exists when you reach a vertex that is still on the current recursion path.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain directed edges u v, meaning u -> v.
extra_fields.output_format: Print CYCLE if a directed cycle exists; otherwise, print ACYCLIC.

questions.title: Lexicographically Smallest Topological Order
questions.objective: Combine Kahn's algorithm with a min-priority queue.
questions.problem_statement:
Given a directed graph, print its lexicographically smallest topological ordering if one exists. Among currently available vertices with indegree zero, always choose the smallest-numbered vertex. If the graph contains a cycle, no topological ordering exists.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-08 — Lexicographically Smallest Topological Order](/diagrams/m19/m19_08.png)

Explanation: Initially 1 and 2 have indegree zero, so choose 1 first. Then choose 2, followed by 3 and 4.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain directed edges u v, meaning u -> v.
questions.output_format: Print the ordering as N vertices separated by single spaces. If the graph contains a cycle, print IMPOSSIBLE.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
No self-loops or duplicate directed edges.
hints: Use a PriorityQueue instead of a plain queue in Kahn's algorithm.
After removing a vertex, decrease the indegree of each successor and add any that reach 0.
If fewer than N vertices are removed, the graph has a cycle.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain directed edges u v, meaning u -> v.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the ordering as N vertices separated by single spaces. If the graph contains a cycle, print IMPOSSIBLE.

questions.title: Shortest Path in an Unweighted Graph
questions.objective: Use BFS layers to compute unweighted shortest distances.
questions.problem_statement:
Find the minimum number of edges in a path from source S to every vertex in an undirected, unweighted graph.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-09 — Shortest Path in an Unweighted Graph](/diagrams/m19/m19_09.png)

Explanation: Vertices 1, 2, and 3 are at distances 0, 1, and 2 from source 1. Vertices 4 and 5 are unreachable.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v. The last line contains S.
questions.output_format: Print N distances in vertex order 1 through N, separated by single spaces. Print -1 for a vertex unreachable from S.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
1 ≤ S ≤ N
No self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: Initialize every distance to -1 and the source's distance to 0.
When BFS discovers v from u, set dist[v] = dist[u] + 1.
BFS finds shortest paths because it reaches every vertex at distance d before any vertex at distance d + 1.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v. The last line contains S.
extra_fields.output_format: Print N distances in vertex order 1 through N, separated by single spaces. Print -1 for a vertex unreachable from S.

questions.title: Dijkstra's Shortest Paths
questions.objective: Compute single-source shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm and a priority queue.
questions.problem_statement:
Given a directed weighted graph with nonnegative edge weights, find the shortest distance from source S to every vertex.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-10 — Dijkstra's Shortest Paths](/diagrams/m19/m19_10.png)

Explanation: The shortest route to 2 is 1 -> 3 -> 2 with cost 2 + 1 = 3. The shortest distance to 4 is 3 + 3 = 6.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain u v w, representing directed edge u -> v with weight w. The last line contains S.
questions.output_format: Print N distances in vertex order 1 through N, separated by single spaces. Print INF for each unreachable vertex.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
0 ≤ w ≤ 10^9
Use 64-bit distances.
No self-loops or duplicate directed edges.
hints: Store (distance, vertex) pairs in a PriorityQueue ordered by distance.
When a pair is removed with a distance larger than the vertex's current best, skip it as stale.
A path can exceed the int range (for example, 4 edges of weight 10^9), so use long.

test_cases.output: INF INF INF INF INF INF 0 INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF INF

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain u v w, representing directed edge u -> v with weight w. The last line contains S.
extra_fields.output_format: Print N distances in vertex order 1 through N, separated by single spaces. Print INF for each unreachable vertex.

questions.title: Minimum Spanning Tree Weight
questions.objective: Build a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal's algorithm and union-find.
questions.problem_statement:
Given an undirected, weighted graph, find the total weight of a minimum spanning tree (MST). An MST connects all vertices with the minimum possible total edge weight and contains exactly N − 1 edges. If the graph is disconnected, no spanning tree exists.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-11 — Minimum Spanning Tree Weight](/diagrams/m19/m19_11.png)

Explanation: Choose the edges with weights 1, 2, and 3 to connect all four vertices. Their total weight is 6.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v w with weight w.
questions.output_format: Print the total MST weight. If the graph is disconnected, print IMPOSSIBLE.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
−10^9 ≤ w ≤ 10^9
The total weight fits in a 64-bit signed integer.
No self-loops or duplicate undirected edges.
hints: Kruskal: sort the edges by weight and add each one whose endpoints are in different DSU sets.
Negative weights need no special handling; sorting still puts the best edges first.
If fewer than N − 1 edges are added, the graph is disconnected. A single vertex has MST weight 0.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v w with weight w.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the total MST weight. If the graph is disconnected, print IMPOSSIBLE.

questions.title: Count Islands in a Grid
questions.objective: Count 4-connected regions of a grid with iterative flood fill.
questions.problem_statement:
A grid contains 1 for land and 0 for water. Count islands, where land cells are connected only horizontally or vertically; diagonal contact does not connect two islands. Use an iterative BFS or DFS to avoid deep recursive calls on large grids.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-12 — Count Islands in a Grid](/diagrams/m19/m19_12.png)

Explanation: There are four separate groups of land: the 2 × 2 block in the top-left corner, the single cell in row 2, the single cell in row 3, and the pair in row 4. Cells that touch only diagonally are not connected, so the answer is 4.
questions.input_format: The first line contains R and C. The next R lines each contain C characters, each either 0 or 1, with no spaces between characters.
questions.output_format: Print the number of islands.
hints: Read each row as a String and look at its characters.
Scan every cell; when you find unvisited land, count a new island and flood-fill it with a queue.
Mark cells as visited when you add them to the queue so no cell is added twice.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains R and C. The next R lines each contain C characters, each either 0 or 1, with no spaces between characters.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the number of islands.

questions.title: Check Whether an Undirected Graph Is Bipartite
questions.objective: Two-color every component with BFS and detect conflicting edges.
questions.problem_statement:
Determine whether the vertices of an undirected graph can be colored using two colors so that every edge connects vertices of different colors. Disconnected components must all be checked. Use BFS or an explicit-stack DFS rather than recursive DFS.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-13 — Check Whether an Undirected Graph Is Bipartite](/diagrams/m19/m19_13.png)

Explanation: A triangle has an odd cycle, so its vertices cannot be assigned two colors while every edge joins different colors.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
questions.output_format: Print YES if the graph is bipartite; otherwise, print NO.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
No self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: Color the start vertex 1 and give every newly discovered neighbor the opposite color.
If an edge joins two vertices of the same color, the graph is not bipartite.
Start a new BFS from every uncolored vertex so that every component is checked.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
extra_fields.output_format: Print YES if the graph is bipartite; otherwise, print NO.

questions.title: Find All Bridges in an Undirected Graph
questions.objective: Find bridges with DFS discovery times and low-link values.
questions.problem_statement:
An edge is a bridge if removing it increases the number of connected components. Print every bridge in an undirected graph. Normalize each bridge as (min(u,v), max(u,v)) and sort the resulting pairs lexicographically.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-14 — Find All Bridges in an Undirected Graph](/diagrams/m19/m19_14.png)

Explanation: Edges 3–4 and 4–5 are the only bridges. Removing either one disconnects part of the graph; the edges of the triangle are not bridges.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
questions.output_format: Print the number of bridges on the first line. Print each bridge as u v on a separate line in lexicographic order. If there are no bridges, print only 0.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 5,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 20,000
No self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: Record disc[u], the time DFS first reaches u, and low[u], the earliest discovery time reachable from u's subtree using at most one back edge.
Tree edge u–v is a bridge exactly when low[v] > disc[u].
Run DFS from every unvisited vertex so that every component is processed.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the number of bridges on the first line. Print each bridge as u v on a separate line in lexicographic order. If there are no bridges, print only 0.

questions.title: Find a Redundant Connection Using DSU
questions.objective: Use union-find to detect the edge that first closes a cycle.
questions.problem_statement:
Edges are added to an initially empty undirected graph in the given order. Exactly one edge creates a cycle when added. Print that first cycle-forming edge using its original input orientation.

Vertex labels are positive integers up to 200,000; they do not have to be consecutive.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-15 — Find a Redundant Connection Using DSU](/diagrams/m19/m19_15.png)

Explanation: After adding 1–2 and 1–3, vertices 2 and 3 are already connected. Adding edge 2–3 creates the cycle.
questions.input_format: The first line contains M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
questions.output_format: Print the first edge that connects two vertices already in the same disjoint set, as u v in its input orientation.
questions.constraints:
3 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
Labels are at most 200,000.
No self-loops or duplicate edges; exactly one redundant edge is guaranteed.
hints: Size the DSU arrays by the largest possible label, 200,000, rather than by M.
For each edge, if find(u) == find(v), that edge is the answer; otherwise, union the two sets.
Print u and v in the order they appeared in the input, not sorted.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the first edge that connects two vertices already in the same disjoint set, as u v in its input orientation.

questions.title: Bellman–Ford with Negative Edges
questions.objective: Relax all edges repeatedly and detect negative cycles reachable from the source.
questions.problem_statement:
Given a directed weighted graph that may contain negative edge weights, find shortest distances from source S using Bellman-Ford. Report a reachable negative-weight cycle if one exists. A negative cycle that cannot be reached from S does not affect the answer.

Self-loops and repeated directed edges may appear. Before relaxing an edge u -> v, skip it if dist[u] is INF; never add an edge weight to the INF sentinel.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-16 — Bellman–Ford with Negative Edges](/diagrams/m19/m19_16.png)

Explanation: The cycle at vertex 4 has negative weight but is unreachable from source 1, so it does not affect source-1 distances.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain u v w, representing u -> v with weight w. The last line contains S.
questions.output_format: If a negative-weight cycle is reachable from S, print NEGATIVE CYCLE. Otherwise, print N distances in vertex order 1 through N, separated by single spaces, using INF for unreachable vertices.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 5,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 20,000
−10^9 ≤ w ≤ 10^9
Self-loops and repeated directed edges are allowed.
Use 64-bit distances.
hints: Relax every edge N − 1 times; you may stop early if a full pass changes nothing.
Then make one more pass: if any edge from a reachable vertex can still be relaxed, a negative cycle is reachable from S.
A zero-weight cycle is not a negative cycle.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain u v w, representing u -> v with weight w. The last line contains S.
extra_fields.output_format: If a negative-weight cycle is reachable from S, print NEGATIVE CYCLE. Otherwise, print N distances in vertex order 1 through N, separated by single spaces, using INF for unreachable vertices.

questions.title: Count Shortest Paths Modulo P
questions.objective: Extend Dijkstra's algorithm to count shortest paths.
questions.problem_statement:
Given a connected undirected graph with strictly positive edge weights, count the number of distinct shortest paths from source S to target T. Two paths are distinct if their edge sequences differ. Return the count modulo P. S and T may be equal; when S = T, count the empty path, so the answer is 1.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-17 — Count Shortest Paths Modulo P](/diagrams/m19/m19_17.png)

Explanation: There are two shortest paths of total weight 2: 1–2–4 and 1–3–4.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N, M, S, T, and P. The next M lines contain edges u v w.
questions.output_format: Print the number of shortest paths from S to T modulo P.
questions.constraints:
2 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
1 ≤ M ≤ 200,000
1 ≤ w ≤ 10^9
2 ≤ P ≤ 2,147,483,647
Use 64-bit distances.
No self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: Run Dijkstra from S and keep ways[v], the number of shortest paths found so far to v.
If a new path to v is strictly shorter, replace ways[v] with ways[u]; if it ties, add ways[u] modulo P.
Because every weight is positive, ways[u] is final when u is removed from the queue with its correct distance.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N, M, S, T, and P. The next M lines contain edges u v w.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the number of shortest paths from S to T modulo P.

questions.title: All-Pairs Shortest Paths (Floyd–Warshall)
questions.objective: Compute all-pairs shortest paths with the Floyd–Warshall triple loop.
questions.problem_statement:
Given a directed weighted graph, compute the shortest distance between every ordered pair of vertices using Floyd–Warshall. A missing edge is represented internally as INF; the distance from a vertex to itself is 0. The input has no negative cycles, no self-loops, and no duplicate directed edges.

During relaxation, skip a pair if either dist[i][k] or dist[k][j] is INF; never add a weight to the INF sentinel.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Explanation: The shortest path from 1 to 3 is 1 -> 2 -> 3 with weight 4 + (−1) = 3, which is better than the direct edge of weight 7.

questions.title: Shortest Path Through a Grid with Obstacles
questions.objective: Apply BFS to a grid to find the fewest moves between two cells.
questions.problem_statement:
Given a grid where 0 is an open cell and 1 is blocked, find the minimum number of moves from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell. You may move up, down, left, or right. If either endpoint is blocked or no route exists, the destination is unreachable.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-19 — Shortest Path Through a Grid with Obstacles](/diagrams/m19/m19_19.png)

Explanation: A shortest route uses five moves: down, right, right, down, right. Other routes of the same length also exist.
questions.input_format: The first line contains R and C. The next R lines contain C integers (0 or 1), separated by spaces.
questions.output_format: Print the minimum number of moves, or -1 if the destination cannot be reached. If the grid is 1 × 1 and open, print 0.
hints: Number each cell r * C + c so the BFS queue can be a plain int array.
Check both endpoints before starting: if either is blocked, the answer is -1.
The distance to a cell is fixed the first time BFS reaches it.

questions.title: Find Articulation Points
questions.objective: Find cut vertices with DFS low-link values and the special root rule.
questions.problem_statement:
A vertex in an undirected graph is an articulation point if removing it and all incident edges increases the number of connected components. Find all articulation points, including across disconnected components.

Graph input rule: Vertices are numbered from 1 to N, and any source or target is between 1 and N. Unless this problem explicitly allows them, the input contains no self-loops or duplicate edges.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes, such as a Node class, without the public keyword.

![M19-20 — Find Articulation Points](/diagrams/m19/m19_20.png)

Explanation: Removing 3 separates the triangle's other vertices from 4 and 5; removing 4 separates vertex 5. Thus the articulation points are 3 and 4.
questions.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
questions.output_format: Print the number of articulation points on the first line. Print their labels in ascending order, separated by single spaces, on the second line. If there are none, print an empty second line.
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 5,000
0 ≤ M ≤ 20,000
No self-loops or duplicate edges.
hints: A non-root vertex u is a cut vertex if some DFS child v has low[v] >= disc[u].
A DFS root is a cut vertex only if it has two or more DFS children.
A vertex may satisfy the condition for several children; count it only once.

extra_fields.input_format: The first line contains N and M. The next M lines contain edges u v.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the number of articulation points on the first line. Print their labels in ascending order, separated by single spaces, on the second line. If there are none, print an empty second line.
